items.original_title: FinancialJuice: Credit Ágricole: FX Weekly

evidence.headline: FinancialJuice: Credit Ágricole: FX Weekly
evidence.snippet: The AI trade has been battered by the Democrat blue wave, concerns about Nvidia’s corporate leadership and the US’s new restrictions on access to advanced chips physically as well as via remote access. Despite US technology stocks being weaker, the USD remains dominant. We hold to the view that the unwinding of the AI trade is bad news for the USD. Much of the currency’s attraction in 2026 has been in investing in US technology stocks rather than USTs. People could argue that the recent price action suggests the USD's safe-haven-with-yield status has returned. Weakening risk sentiment is a significant positive for the USD vs the CAD, GBP, AUD, NZD, NOK and JPY. It is not important for the USD’s performance vs the EUR, CHF or SEK. Importantly, risk sentiment is a bigger driver than rates for only GBP/USD and is equally important to rates for AUD/USD. So the jump in US rates is behind most of the USD's recent strength rather than a run to the currency as a safe haven. Sovereign risk remains more important than general risk for EUR/USD and USD/SEK. For USD/JPY, sovereign risk is a bigger driver than general risk sentiment, but rates are the largest driver of the exchange rate. This matters for the coming week as economic performance and inflation will be compared across G10 currencies. The US, UK and Eurozone see the releases of PMI as well German IFO and US consumer confidence data. French and Spanish inflation data will be compared with US core PCE data. Australian inflation could remain stubborn which could risk whipsawing investors after weak labour market data. items.original_title: FinancialJuice: Deutsche Bank: Chips and the USD

evidence.headline: FinancialJuice: Deutsche Bank: Chips and the USD
evidence.snippet: What do chips have to do with a new era of dollar dominance? As we discuss in this paper - a great deal. Chips are not only critical to the future of AI but have recently emerged as a huge driver of global trade and capital flows. It is well known that the US is dominant in upstream chip technology and downstream compute. This note delves deeper into the workings of the middle of the chain where flows have been reinforcing the dollar's global role. The manufacturing of chips largely takes place in Asia where chip-related trade surpluses have ballooned. As we show, these surpluses are finding their way back to the US via investments in US capital markets. Asian chip surpluses are not being recycled into US Treasuries like petrodollar surpluses were, but into US equities. Foreign inflows into US equities have crossed USDItn a year and become the mainstay of US deficit funding. The biggest source of increase over the past year has come from Asia. Equity flows have not just been supporting the US dollar but have provided financing to the companies driving the AI buildout and chips boom itself. This introduces forms of circularity and potential instability to global flows. Moreover, equities are a much riskier asset class than bonds - US stocks are three times as volatile as Treasuries, with tech stocks up to ten times as much. Growing dollar dependence on inherently riskier capital should spill into higher US dollar volatility over time. The rise of chips as a driver of dollar dominance can be seen as a symptom of change in the ultimate source of US power - from geopolitical to technological leadership.
